Char: Methods:
Randomised controlled trial 

Trial conducted from January 2012 to March 2013
Char: Participants:
453 adolescent girls 11-18 years residing in Jhuggi Jhompri cluster, urban slum at Kirti Nagar, New Delhi, India

Inclusion criteria: Mild (Hb 100–119 g/l) or moderately (Hb 70–99 g/l) anaemic unmarried adolescent girls (11-18 years; still reside with parents i.e. prior to Gauna); and willingness to participate in study

Exclusion criteria: Severe anemia, pregnancy, severe medical condition, e.g. Tuberculosis or Cancer
Char: Interventions:
Intervention (n = 227): vitamin B12 supplementation (500 µg/week for 6 weeks and 15 µg/week for 20 weeks) plus IFA ( iron 100 mg, folic acid 500 µg)

Control (n = 226): IFA alone ( iron 100 mg, folic acid 500 µg)

Duration: 26 weeks

All children received deworming tablets containing 400 mg Albendazole before initiation of supplementation.
Char: Outcomes:
Primary outcomes: Hemoglobin concentrations at baseline and at 6 months

Secondary outcomes:  Serum ferritin, serum folic acid, serum vitamin B12, and C-reactive protein concentrations at baseline and at 6 months. Weight, height, and body mass index at baseline.
Char: Notes:
Compliance: administered by study volunteers under supervision of the investigator with a spare day kept within the week in case the study volunteer was not available on the main day of the supplementation. To ensure 100% compliance, a tentative time table of the study volunteer’s activities during evening was also maintained, and they were followed in their ‘Tuition classes’, ‘Salai Centres’, etc. for the supplementation. Results not reported

Anaemia status at start of supplementation: all participants were anaemic at the start of study

Vitamin B12 status at start of supplementation: Intervention: 63.3%; Control: 63.6% (serum vitamin B12 < 203 pg/mL)

Vitamin B12 compound: cyanocobalamin

Funding source: M/s Cyano Pharma Private Limited, Indore (Madhya Pradesh), provided supplements required for the trial

Declarations of interest: no conflict of interest reported

Ethical approval: Ethics Committee Clearance was obtained from Lady Irwin College, University of Delhi. Permissions were also obtained from the Drug Controller General of India

Study is not included in review because no disaggregated data are available for children < 12 years (age group: 11-18 years). Trial authors were contacted for additional information (pending).

Char: Participants:
150 children were 6 months to 5 years old and were recruited from the Department of Pediatrics and Pathology, Lady Hardinge Medical College associated with the Kalawati Saran Children's Hospital, New Delhi, India. Children were allocated to 1 of 2 groups.

Inclusion criteria: Age 6 months to 5 years, hemoglobin less than normal for age as per WHO criteria, clinical diagnosis of nutritional anemia based on history and physical examination, and no other significant cause of anemia (e.g. malaria) by history and physical examination.

Exclusion criteria: Children with chronic illness, having other associated hematological disorders, receiving hematopoietic micronutrient supplementation or having received blood products
Char: Interventions:
Intervention (n = 74): vitamin B12 supplementation (125 μg, 250 μg and 500 μg oral vitamin B12 as tablets daily for children under 1 year, 1–2 years or older than 2 years, respectively or 250 μg or 500 μg vitamin B12 injection every 2 weeks for children younger than 2 years and 2–5 years, respectively) plus iron and folic acid tablets (200 mg elemental iron + 0.1mg folic acid + 2.5 or 5 mg folic acid for < 2 year- and > 2 year-old children, respectively)

Control (n = 76): iron plus folic acid alone (200 mg elemental iron + 0.1mg FA + 2.5 or 5mg FA for < 2 year- and > 2 year-olde children, respectively)

Duration: 8 weeks

For the purposes of this review, we will compare children receiving oral vitamin B12 supplementation versus IFA only.
Char: Outcomes: Haemoglobin concentration (follow-up assessments were conducted at 2, 4, and at 8 weeks)
Char: Notes:
Compliance: monitored by checking returned and empty packs at follow-up visit; results not reported

Anaemia status at start of supplementation: not reported separately for children receiving oral vitamin B12 supplementation

Vitamin B12 status at start of supplementation: not reported

Vitamin B12 compound: methylcobalamin

Funding source: not reported

Declarations of interest: not reported

Ethical approval: Approval from the Institutional Review Board was obtained to conduct the trial.

Study is not included in review because no disaggregated data were available for children who received oral vitamin B12 supplementation. Trial authors were contacted for additional information (pending).

Char: Participants:
170 children, 10-16 years old attending four Jena schools (4 to 6 from each class) in Germany. Children were assigned to 1 of 2 groups. 

Inclusion criteria: children were included in the trial if teachers identified their school performance was reduced as a result of nervous behavioral disorders and lack of concentration.
Char: Outcomes: Weight, length, cognitive function (concentration progression test by Abels, letter strikethrough test according to Bourdon, modified number symbol test according to Hamburg-Wechsler, and ability to concentrate and absolute school results measured via teacher's  judgement), fatigue and balance (measured via teacher's judgement), all assessed at 5 months
Char: Notes:
Compliance: not reported

Anaemia status at start of supplementation: not reported

Vitamin B12 status at start of supplementation: not reported

Vitamin B12 compound: cyanocobalamin

Funding source: not reported

Declarations of interest: not reported

Ethical approval: not reported

Study record was translated from German to English.

Study is not included in review because no disaggregated data were available for children < 12 years (age group: 10-16 years). Contact information for trial authors inaccurate or out-of-date; correspondence not successful.

Char: Methods:
Randomised controlled trial 

Trial conducted from 1 July 2010 to 30 June 2011
Char: Participants:
100 children, 6-36 months of age, less than or equal to 3 standard deviations below weight-for-height growth standards

Inclusion criteria: children less than or equal to 3 standard deviations below weight-for-height growth standards

Exclusion criteria: children with an acute illness or an incapacitating congenital malformation
Char: Interventions:
Intervention: vitamin B12 plus multiple micronutrients daily

Control: multiple micronutrients alone daily

Duration: 6 months
Char: Outcomes:
Primary outcomes: Total body water measured by D2O dilution method at baseline and visit 5. Bio-impedance analysis  at baseline and visit 5. 

Secondary outcomes: Anthropometric measurements at baseline and visit 5. Hematological analysis at baseline and visit 5.
Char: Notes:
Ethics approval: KEM Hospital Research Centre's Ethics Committee approved on the 23rd July 2009 (ref: KEMHRC/VSP/Dir Off/EC/1005)

Funding source: International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) (Austria), KEM Hospital and Research Centre (India) - Diabetes Unit

This record is a trials registry for a randomised controlled trial in India. The study is not included in this review because no associated reports or published data are available. We will evaluate available data for incusion in future updates of this review.

Char: Participants:
955 male and female children, 4-16 years were recruited from rural communities in the parishes of St. Thomas and St. Andrews, and in orphanages in Jamaica. Children were assigned to 1 of 2 groups.

Inclusion criteria: Children regularly attending school, each sex and growth type based on the Wetzel grid (categorizes children into five groups on the basis of physique)

Trial authors report analysis was limited to children ≤ 12 years (n = 523; average age: 9.6 years) to limit the impact of puberty on increased growth rate.
Char: Interventions:
Intervention (n = 133): vitamin B12 suppmentation (100  µg/day)

Control (n = 134): placebo

Duration: 2 years during school attendance days only
Char: Outcomes: Weight, height at baseline, monthly, and at 2 years
Char: Notes:
Compliance: administered at school; results not reported

Anaemia status at start of supplementation: not reported  

Vitamin B12 status at start of supplementation: not reported

Vitamin B12 compound: not reported

Funding source: Grants from Lederle and Co., Pearl River, New York, and Merck and Co., Rahway, New Jersey.

Declarations of interest: not reported

Ethical approval: not reported

This trial is not included in this review due to no disaggregated data for children < 12 years (age group: children 12 years and under). Contact information for trial authors inaccurate or out-of-date; correspondence not successful

Char: Participants:
Population: 25 children, over the age of 1 year, with iron deficiency anemia (IDA)

Inclusion criteria: iron deficiency anaemia regardless of the etiology. IDA defined as Hb < 11 g/dL; blood value < 33%; mean corpuscular volume < 70µ3; mean corpuscular haemoglobin ≤ 35%; transferrin saturation < 16%; transferrinaemia > 350 mg%; serum iron < 60 mg%; and free internal erythrocyte protoporphyrin < 15 mg%.
Char: Interventions:
Intervention (n = 9): daily iron and vitamin B12 supplementation (40 mg ferritin plus 1 mg adenosyl cobamide coenzyme)

Intervention (n = 9): daily iron, folic acid and vitamin B12 supplementation (40 mg ferritin, 400 mcg folinic acid and 1 mg adenosyl cobamide coenzyme)

Control (n = 7): daily iron supplementation alone (40 mg ferritin)

Duration: 60 days

For the purposes of this review we will compare children receiving oral vitamin B12 and iron to iron supplementation only.
Char: Outcomes: Haemoglobin concentration, mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular haemoglobin, transferrin saturation, transferrinaemia, serum iron, ferritin, and free internal erythrocyte protoporphyrin. Hospitalizations and the general well-being. All outcomes were assessed at 15, 30 and 60 days.
Char: Notes:
Anaemia status at start of supplementation: all participants were anaemic at the start of study

Vitamin B12 compound: adenosyl cobamide coenzyme

This trial is not included in this review due to insufficient information on study characteristics and no disaggregated data for children (age group: over the age of 10 years). Contact information for trial authors inaccurate or out-of-date; correspondence not successful
